subject: Medicine
summary: Oesophageal varices are dilated veins in the distal oesophagus caused by portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis. They bleed massively and require urgent recognition and treatment. Management balances bleeding control, infection prevention and long‑term portal pressure reduction.

sections.p: Oesophageal varices are submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus that become enlarged when portal pressure rises. Diagnosis is confirmed by upper GI endoscopy, which visualises the varices and grades their size.

t.b: Shows variceal size and presence of red signs; determines need for band ligation
Assesses portal vein diameter and hepatic vein flow; indicates portal hypertension
Visualises splenomegaly, collaterals and liver morphology when endoscopy is contraindicated

sections.p: Severity is staged by the Baveno criteria and the Child‑Pugh score. The Baveno IV stage (large varices or red signs) predicts high bleeding risk.
b: Baveno IV: large varices or red signs

t.b: Classifies liver function; higher class correlates with variceal bleeding risk

sections.p: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis is the leading cause. Alcoholic liver disease is the most common etiology, followed by viral hepatitis and schistosomiasis in endemic areas.

t.b: Elevated bilirubin and transaminases suggest liver injury; hypoalbuminaemia indicates chronic disease
Identifies viral etiology; guides antiviral therapy

sections.p: Patients often have no symptoms until bleeding. Acute haematemesis, coffee‑ground vomitus, or melena are classic. Chronic bleeding may present as iron‑deficiency anaemia.

t.b: Low levels indicate chronic blood loss
Thrombocytopenia reflects splenic sequestration; severe drop raises bleeding risk

sections.p: Investigations confirm portal hypertension, assess liver function and rule out other causes of upper GI bleeding.

t.b: Detects varices and red signs; guides band ligation
Measures portal vein diameter; detects splenomegaly

sections.p: Red flags include massive haematemesis, hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status. Complications are rebleeding, hepatic encephalopathy and infection.

t.b: Prolonged PT/INR signals coagulopathy; high INR increases bleeding risk

sections.p: Initial resuscitation, vasoactive drugs, antibiotics, and endoscopic band ligation are mandatory. Long‑term therapy targets portal pressure with beta‑blockers or endoscopic therapy.

t.b: Reduce portal pressure; avoid in severe heart failure
Vasoconstricts splanchnic vessels; monitor renal function

sections.p: Regular endoscopic surveillance every 6–12 months in high‑risk patients. Vaccination for hepatitis B, alcohol cessation, and treatment of underlying liver disease reduce recurrence.

t.b: Prevents re‑infection and progression of liver disease

sections.p: Non‑variceal upper GI bleeding such as peptic ulcer disease, Mallory–Weiss tear, and gastritis.
Normal platelet count can mask thrombocytopenia if splenomegaly is present. Mildly elevated liver enzymes may be normal in early cirrhosis.

t.b: A normal count does not exclude portal hypertension if splenomegaly is present
